q: In paper chromatography, which substance in a mixture travels the furthest up the paper?
options: the one most soluble in the solvent and least attracted to the paper
the one least soluble in the solvent and most attracted to the paper
the one with the darkest colour
the one that is the most dense
explain: A substance that dissolves well in the solvent and sticks weakly to the paper is carried further by the moving solvent.

q: A black ink is tested by chromatography and gives four separate coloured spots. What does this show?
options: The ink is a single pure substance.
The ink contains at least four different coloured substances.
The ink contains exactly one dye in four forms.
The ink is insoluble in the solvent.
explain: Each separate spot is a different substance, so there are at least four. Two substances with identical movement would overlap into one spot.

q: The beaker used for chromatography is often covered with a lid. Why?
options: to make the solvent move faster up the paper
to stop the solvent evaporating from the beaker
to keep the paper dry
to stop the dyes being seen
explain: The lid keeps the air saturated with solvent vapour, so the solvent does not evaporate from the paper and the run is more reliable.

q: Some coloured dyes are insoluble in water. What can be done to separate them by paper chromatography?
options: Use a thicker piece of paper.
Heat the paper until the dyes dissolve.
Use a different suitable solvent, such as ethanol.
Use ink instead of the dyes.
explain: The solvent must dissolve the substances to be separated, so if water does not dissolve them another solvent such as ethanol is chosen.

q: Which observation on a chromatogram is evidence that a substance is impure?
options: It forms more than one spot.
It forms one spot that is not at the solvent front.
It forms a single coloured spot.
It stays on the starting line.
explain: A pure substance produces one spot. More than one spot means more than one substance is present.

q: Which method can be used to show that a green ink is a mixture of dyes?
options: filtration
evaporation to dryness
crystallisation
paper chromatography with a suitable solvent
explain: Chromatography separates soluble coloured substances so each dye appears as a separate spot. The other methods do not separate dyes.

q: What is a chromatogram?
options: the solvent that moves up the paper
the paper showing the positions of the separated substances after the run
the line on which the mixture is first placed
the substance that does not move
explain: A chromatogram is the paper record of the separation: the spots show where each substance finished.

q: Amino acids are colourless. What must be done to see their positions on a chromatogram?
options: Run the chromatogram in the dark.
Use a thicker piece of paper.
Add more of the amino acids to the starting line.
Spray the paper with a locating agent that reacts with them to form coloured spots.
explain: Colourless substances cannot be seen on the paper, so a locating agent that reacts with them to give a colour is applied after the run.

q: On a chromatogram a spot travels 3.6 cm while the solvent travels 7.2 cm. What is the Rf value?
explain: Rf = distance travelled by the substance ÷ distance travelled by the solvent = 3.6 ÷ 7.2 = 0.50.

q: The solvent front moves 8.0 cm up the paper. A substance has an Rf value of 0.35. How far does the substance travel?
options: 2.8 cm
explain: Distance = Rf × solvent distance = 0.35 × 8.0 = 2.8 cm.

q: Which statement about Rf values is correct?
options: An Rf value is measured in cm and can be larger than 1.
An Rf value is larger when the substance is less soluble in the solvent.
An Rf value is the distance moved by the solvent divided by that moved by the substance.
An Rf value has no units and cannot be greater than 1.
explain: Rf is a ratio of two distances, so it has no units. The substance can never travel further than the solvent, so Rf is never greater than 1.

q: In one solvent, substances W, X, Y and Z have Rf values 0.25, 0.40, 0.55 and 0.80. In the same solvent an unknown spot travels 2.2 cm while the solvent front travels 5.5 cm. Which substance is it?
options: W
Y
X
Z
explain: Rf of the unknown = 2.2 ÷ 5.5 = 0.40, which matches substance X.

q: A student stops a chromatography run earlier than planned, with the same paper and solvent. What happens to the Rf value of a substance?
options: It decreases because the substance has moved a shorter distance.
It stays the same because both distances change in the same proportion.
It increases because the solvent has moved a shorter distance.
It becomes zero.
explain: Rf is the ratio of the two distances. Stopping earlier shortens both distances proportionally, so the ratio is unchanged.

q: In the same solvent, substance P has an Rf value of 0.72 and substance Q has an Rf value of 0.31. Which statement is correct?
options: P is more soluble in the solvent or less attracted to the paper than Q.
Q travelled further than P.
P is less soluble in the solvent than Q.
P and Q must be the same substance.
explain: The higher Rf value means P travelled further relative to the solvent. That occurs when it dissolves better in the solvent or sticks less to the paper.

q: Which technique separates undissolved chalk powder from water?
options: simple distillation
crystallisation
fractional distillation
filtration
explain: The chalk is insoluble, so it stays on the filter paper as the residue while the water passes through as the filtrate.

q: Which method is used to obtain crystals of copper(II) sulfate from a solution of copper(II) sulfate?
options: Heat the solution until all the water has evaporated.
Heat the solution to evaporate some of the water, then leave it to cool so that crystals form.
Filter the solution and keep the filtrate.
Distil the solution and collect the distillate.
explain: Partly evaporating the water gives a hot saturated solution; on cooling the solubility falls, so crystals form. Distilling would collect water, not crystals.

q: In a simple distillation apparatus, how should cooling water pass through the condenser?
options: in at the top and out at the bottom, so that the jacket drains quickly
in and out at the same level
in at the bottom and out at the top, so that the jacket stays full of water
in at the bottom and out through the flask
explain: Water entering at the bottom rises and fills the jacket, so the condenser stays cold along its whole length.

q: A mixture of ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water (boiling point 100 °C) is heated in fractional distillation apparatus. Which liquid is collected first?
options: ethanol, because it has the lower boiling point
water, because it has the higher boiling point
ethanol, because it is denser
water, because it has the lower relative molecular mass
explain: The liquid with the lower boiling point evaporates and reaches the top of the column first, so ethanol is collected first.

q: A mixture contains sand and sodium chloride. Which sequence of steps separates both substances?
options: Add water and stir, filter, then evaporate the filtrate to obtain the salt.
Heat the mixture strongly and collect the vapour.
Filter the dry mixture and then add water to the filtrate.
Add water, evaporate the mixture, then filter the residue.
explain: Salt dissolves and sand does not. Filtering removes the sand as the residue, and evaporating the salt solution leaves solid sodium chloride.

q: A student heats an unknown solid and it melts completely between 120 °C and 126 °C. The pure compound melts at 130 °C. What can be concluded?
options: The sample is pure.
The sample is a different pure substance.
The sample is an element.
The sample is impure.
explain: A pure substance melts sharply at its fixed melting point. Impurities lower the melting point and make the solid melt over a range of temperatures.

q: A colourless liquid boils over the range 78–84 °C. What does this suggest?
options: The liquid is a pure substance.
The liquid is an element.
The liquid is a mixture.
The liquid is a solid dissolved in water.
explain: A pure liquid boils at one fixed temperature. A range of boiling temperatures shows that more than one substance is present.

q: Which row correctly describes how a pure solid and an impure solid melt?
options: melts over a range of temperatures | melts at one sharp temperature
melts at one sharp temperature | melts over a range of temperatures
melts at one sharp temperature | melts at a higher sharp temperature
melts over a range of temperatures | melts over a range at a higher temperature
explain: A pure solid has a sharp melting point. Impurities usually lower the melting point and spread the melting over a range.

q: What is the purpose of the glass beads or rings in a fractionating column?
options: They stop the liquid from boiling.
They react with the vapours.
They keep the column hot at the top.
They provide a large surface area for repeated condensing and evaporating.
explain: Vapour condenses on the large surface and re-evaporates repeatedly, so the vapour that reaches the top is richer in the more volatile liquid.

q: A mixture of three miscible liquids X (boiling point 65 °C), Y (82 °C) and Z (118 °C) is separated by fractional distillation. In which order are they collected?
options: X, then Y, then Z
Z, then Y, then X
Y, then X, then Z
X, Y and Z all together
explain: Liquids distil in order of increasing boiling point, so the one with the lowest boiling point (X) is collected first.

q: Why is crystallisation by cooling a hot saturated solution preferred to evaporating all the water from copper(II) sulfate solution to obtain hydrated crystals?
options: Cooling makes the crystals dissolve in the solvent.
Evaporating to dryness makes the crystals blue.
Evaporating to dryness would drive off the water of crystallisation and could leave impurities mixed in the solid.
Evaporating to dryness is not possible with water.
explain: Heating strongly removes the water that is part of the hydrated crystals. Crystallising from a saturated solution gives larger, purer crystals.

q: A mixture of sodium chloride and sand is separated by adding water. Which property difference makes this possible?
options: Sand has a lower melting point than sodium chloride.
Sodium chloride is soluble in water but sand is not.
Sodium chloride is magnetic but sand is not.
Sand is denser than water but sodium chloride is not.
explain: Adding a suitable solvent dissolves only the soluble substance, which allows the insoluble substance to be removed by filtration.

q: Aqueous sodium chloride boils at 103 °C at normal atmospheric pressure. What does this show?
options: It is pure water, because boiling points vary.
It is pure water at higher pressure.
It is pure sodium chloride.
It is not pure water, because the dissolved salt raises the boiling point.
explain: Pure water boils at 100 °C at normal pressure. Dissolved impurities raise the boiling point, so 103 °C shows the liquid is a solution.

q: Seawater is separated by simple distillation. What collects in the receiving flask?
options: pure water, as the distillate
salt, as the residue
seawater with less salt
a mixture of salt and water vapour
explain: Water evaporates and condenses in the condenser, so it is collected as the distillate. The salt stays in the distillation flask.

q: In a simple distillation, where should the bulb of the thermometer be placed?
options: in the liquid at the bottom of the flask
in the condenser
level with the side arm of the flask, in the vapour
in the receiving flask
explain: The thermometer is meant to read the temperature of the vapour that is about to leave the flask, which is the boiling point of the liquid.

q: Four pure solids melt at these temperatures: P 41 °C, Q 80 °C, R 114 °C, S 135 °C. An unknown pure solid melts sharply at 80 °C. Which is it most likely to be?
options: P
Q
R
S
explain: A pure substance has a specific melting point, so an unknown that melts sharply at 80 °C is most likely to be Q.
